newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No Chechen secession after Lebed deal - Chernomyrdin.
newsitem.headline: No Chechen secession after Lebed deal - Chernomyrdin.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin issued a stern reminder on Saturday that Moscow would not yield to independence demands from Chechnya following a peace accord reached two weeks ago.

"The resolution of all these complex issues must be based only on the constitution of the Russian Federation and on the principle of the territorial integrity of Russia," the government press service said.
The statement, issued after a meeting chaired by the prime minister, will not please the separatist rebels in the region.
Their leader, Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, has insisted that a referendum on independence will eventually lead to secession.

Chernomyrdin, who has taken on extra tasks while President Boris Yeltsin prepares for heart surgery, said the meeting was to decide on routes to a lasting peace following Lebed's accord. He described it last week as merely "a statement of intention".
The gathering may also mark a bid to rein in Yeltsin's personal envoy Alexander Lebed, who signed the peace deal.

In the absence of the president, who is spending the weekend in a Moscow clinic for pre-operative tests, speculation is rife that Chernomyrdin and Lebed, an ambitious political outsider, are among key figures jockeying for power in the Kremlin.

The government press service said the talks, which included Lebed and Yeltsin's influential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, covered the formation of a transitional regional government for Chechnya and tightening up security in the province.

It said Chernomyrdin charged some officials with new tasks but did not say what these were. He said on Friday that a full legal settlement and federal reconstruction funds would have to wait until there was a provisional government in Grozny.

Lebed, who was named Kremlin security chief by Yeltsin in June, agreed with the rebels at Khasav-Yurt on August 31 to withdraw Russian troops and defer for five years the resolution of the separatists' demands for independence.
Implicitly, therefore, he left the issue open.
Chernomyrdin gave the deal a cool response and has already stressed the deal is not legally binding. Other ministers say they are worried Lebed did not do enough to rule out secession.

The officials decided to hold weekly meetings, a move that appeared close to resurrecting a defunct committee on Chechnya, chaired by Chernomyrdin, which Yeltsin disbanded last month when he put Lebed in sole charge of ending the conflict.
Lebed told the meeting: "It is essential to decide with collective wisdom what steps should be taken to settle the Chechen crisis after the signing of the Khasav-Yurt accords."

But the sight of him sitting in committee with Chernomyrdin and other ministers in Moscow was a sharp contrast to last month's dramatic solo flights to Chechnya to stop an outbreak of fighting and win the trust of the separatist leadership.

In Chechnya, a three-way conflict has been brewing between Russian troops, the separatist rebels who seized the capital Grozny last month and the pro-Moscow Chechen administration, which Lebed pointedly left out of his peace settlement.
A Russian military spokesman told Itar-Tass news agency a separatist commander was shot dead in a dispute with pro-Moscow Chechens in the predominantly loyalist north of the region.
Another told Interfax news agency that separatists had shot at a guard post near Grozny's Severny airport and accused the rebels of trying to provoke a conflict.
The Russian commander in the region suspended planned troop withdrawals almost as soon as they had begun last week, complaining of disputes over the exchange of prisoners.
Separatist spokesman Movladi Udugov told Tass some generals were making "extraordinarily dangerous" attempts to revise the peace deal which was undermining trust among his fighters.
In Grozny, Russian forces and separatist delegates met to try to discuss a variety of complaints on either side.
